items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: Ecologists are mapping a restored wetland. Two straight boundary paths, line $j$ and line $k$, are both crossed by a straight drainage ditch, line $t$. Line $t$ meets line $j$ at point $A$ and meets line $k$ at point $B$, with $B$ below $A$. At point $A$, angle 1 is above line $j$ and to the right of line $t$, angle 2 is above line $j$ and to the left of line $t$, and angle 3 is below line $j$ and to the left of line $t$. At point $B$, angle 5 is above line $k$ and to the right of line $t$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $j$ is parallel to line $k$?
items.explanation: Angle 1 and angle 5 are in the same position at the two crossings: above their path and to the right of the ditch. That makes them corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel, so this fact is enough.

A.why: Angles 1 and 3 are vertical angles at the same crossing, and vertical angles are always equal whenever two lines cross. Because this is true whether or not $j$ and $k$ are parallel, it can't prove that they are.

B.why: Angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair along line $j$, so they always add to $180^\circ$. You used the supplementary rule, but it only proves parallel lines when it applies to same-side interior angles at two different crossings.

D.why: Saying angle 1 equals angle 2 only tells you that each is $90^\circ$, so the ditch is perpendicular to line $j$. It tells you nothing about line $k$, so it doesn't compare the two paths at all.
